title: Classical ML Mid-Term
description: 20 questions covering regression, gradient descent, decision trees, ensembles, and evaluation.

questions.question: Which loss function does Linear Regression minimize?
questions.explanation: Linear regression minimizes MSE (mean squared error). Squaring errors penalizes large mistakes more, which encourages a good overall fit.

questions.question: In gradient descent, what happens if the learning rate is too large?
options: Training is slower but always converges
The loss may oscillate or diverge instead of converging
questions.explanation: A learning rate that's too large causes the optimizer to overshoot the minimum. The loss bounces around or climbs instead of falling.

questions.question: Logistic regression outputs a probability between 0 and 1.
questions.explanation: Yes — the sigmoid function squashes any real number into (0, 1), which we interpret as the probability of the positive class.

questions.question: What is the decision boundary of a logistic regression model?
options: A linear surface where the predicted probability equals 0.5
The midpoint between the two class centroids
questions.explanation: The decision boundary is where σ(wᵀx + b) = 0.5, which means wᵀx + b = 0 — a hyperplane.

questions.question: At each node, a Decision Tree splits by choosing the feature and threshold that:
options: Maximizes accuracy on the full training set
Minimizes the depth of the tree
Maximizes information gain (or minimizes Gini impurity) in the child nodes
questions.explanation: Decision Trees use a greedy, local criterion — they pick whatever split produces the purest child nodes, measured by information gain or Gini.

questions.question: A deep, unpruned Decision Tree with no min-samples constraint will almost always overfit training data.
questions.explanation: An unconstrained tree can memorize every training example by splitting until each leaf has exactly one sample. It gets 100% train accuracy but generalizes poorly.

questions.question: What key idea makes Random Forest different from a single Decision Tree?
options: It trains many trees on random subsets of data and features, then averages predictions
It replaces the tree with a neural network
It uses a different loss function
questions.explanation: Random Forest uses bootstrap sampling (bagging) and random feature subsets for each tree. Averaging many diverse trees reduces variance without increasing bias much.

questions.question: Gradient Boosting builds trees sequentially. Each new tree is trained on:
options: The residuals (errors) of the previous ensemble
questions.explanation: Gradient Boosting fits each new tree to the gradient of the loss — effectively the residuals. Each tree corrects mistakes the ensemble has made so far.

questions.question: In a classification problem where only 1% of samples are positive, accuracy is not a good metric because:
options: Accuracy can't be computed for imbalanced classes
A model predicting 'negative' for everything achieves 99% accuracy while being useless
Accuracy is always worse than AUC
questions.explanation: With class imbalance, a trivial model that always predicts the majority class gets near-perfect accuracy. Use precision, recall, or F1 instead.

questions.question: Which metric is the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall?
questions.explanation: F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall). Harmonic mean means F1 is only high when BOTH precision and recall are high.

questions.question: A model with high AUC-ROC (e.g., 0.95) always has high accuracy.
questions.explanation: AUC measures ranking quality, not accuracy at a fixed threshold. On imbalanced datasets, high AUC can coexist with poor accuracy — and vice versa.

questions.question: Feature scaling (e.g., StandardScaler) is most critical for which algorithm?
questions.explanation: Tree-based models split on thresholds so scale doesn't matter. Gradient-based models like logistic regression converge much faster when features are on the same scale.

questions.question: One-hot encoding is used to:
options: Convert a categorical feature into multiple binary columns
questions.explanation: One-hot encoding creates one binary column per category. It lets linear models and distance-based models work with categorical data without implying an ordinal relationship.

questions.question: L2 regularization (Ridge) adds the sum of squared weights to the loss, which pushes weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero.
questions.explanation: L2 penalizes large weights smoothly (it's differentiable everywhere). L1 (Lasso) uses absolute values and can set weights exactly to zero, making it a feature selector.

questions.question: What is the bias-variance tradeoff?
options: High bias → overfitting; high variance → underfitting
High bias → underfitting; high variance → overfitting
Both bias and variance should always be minimized together
Bias and variance are independent and have no tradeoff
questions.explanation: A simple model has high bias (underfits, misses patterns). A complex model has high variance (overfits, sensitive to training noise). You balance them with regularization and data.

questions.question: k-fold cross-validation with k=5 trains how many separate models?
questions.explanation: 5-fold CV splits data into 5 folds, trains on 4 and validates on 1, rotating which fold is the held-out set. That's 5 training runs and 5 validation scores.

questions.question: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) updates weights using:
options: The gradient computed on all training data
The gradient computed on one (or a mini-batch of) training examples
questions.explanation: SGD uses a single example or small mini-batch per update. It's noisier than full-batch GD but much faster per update and can escape shallow local minima.

questions.question: Increasing the depth of a decision tree always decreases training error.
questions.explanation: Deeper trees can always split further, eventually memorizing each training point. Training error monotonically decreases with depth — but validation error usually increases after a point.

questions.question: In IOAI competitions, XGBoost and LightGBM are popular because:
options: They are fast, handle missing values, and perform well on tabular data
They are the only algorithms allowed in IOAI
questions.explanation: Gradient boosting libraries (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) dominate tabular competitions because they're fast, handle heterogeneous features, and tune well with fewer data.

questions.question: You train a model and get: Train accuracy = 99%, Validation accuracy = 61%. This is most likely:
options: Underfitting — the model is too simple
Overfitting — the model memorized training data
A good result — high train accuracy is the goal
A data leakage problem — impossible otherwise
questions.explanation: A huge gap between train and validation performance is the classic overfitting signature. Fix it with regularization, more data, dropout, or a simpler model.
